target_audience: Undergraduate students or advanced high school students with basic calculus knowledge

sections.title: The Shift: From Counting to Measuring
sections.content: Introduce the difference between discrete variables (things you count) and continuous variables (things you measure). Explain why we can't assign a specific probability to a single point in a continuous range (the 'Zero Probability Paradox').
sections.example: Meet 'Pip the Robot'. If Pip flips a coin, there are 2 outcomes. But if Pip measures the exact time a lightbulb lasts, there are infinite possible values (e.g., 100.1 hours, 100.125 hours). The probability of it lasting exactly 100.000... hours is effectively zero.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Smoothing Histogram
sections.content: Review the concept of a histogram where bar area represents frequency. Show how, as the number of data points increases and the bin width decreases to nearly zero, the jagged bars transform into a smooth continuous curve.
sections.example: Visualizing a histogram of 1,000 cheetahs' running speeds. As we measure more cheetahs with more precision, the 'steps' of the graph smooth out into a continuous wave-like shape.

sections.title: Defining the PDF: Height vs. Area
sections.content: Define the Probability Density Function, f(x). Crucially, explain that the height f(x) is NOT the probability. Instead, the 'Area under the curve' between two points represents the probability of the event falling in that range.
sections.example: A graphical plot where the x-axis is 'Cheetah Speed' and the y-axis is 'Density'. Shading the region between 60 km/h and 70 km/h represents the probability of a cheetah running at a speed within that specific interval.

sections.title: The Golden Rules of PDFs
sections.content: Present the two mathematical constraints: 1) The function f(x) must never be negative (you can't have negative probability density). 2) The total area under the entire curve must equal exactly 1 (representing 100% total probability).
sections.example: An animation showing a spotlight shining on a curve. No matter how the curve is shaped (tall and thin or short and wide), a 'Total Area = 1' counter stays constant at the bottom of the screen.

sections.title: Application: The Delivery Drone
sections.content: Synthesize the knowledge by calculating the probability of a real-world event using a simple PDF shape (like a uniform or normal distribution). Show the integration (area calculation) visually.
sections.example: A delivery drone is expected to arrive within a 10-minute window. We use a rectangular (Uniform) PDF. To find the probability the drone arrives in the first 2 minutes, we calculate the area of that specific 2-minute slice of the rectangle.

sections.title: Summary and Key Takeaway
sections.content: Reiterate that PDFs allow us to handle the 'infinite' nature of the real world. Remind students: In a PDF world, Area = Probability.
sections.example: A quick visual recap showing Pip the Robot looking at a bell curve, highlighting a shaded slice, and a math sign popping up saying: Area = P(a < X < b).
